title: Sensitivity and specificity of medical tests
intro: No medical test is perfect. Sensitivity and specificity describe how well a test finds people with a disease and how well it correctly clears people without it. Understanding these ideas helps you interpret results, particularly from screening, and see why a positive result is not always a diagnosis.

sections.heading: Sensitivity
paragraphs: Sensitivity is the proportion of people with the disease whom the test correctly identifies as positive. A test with ninety percent sensitivity detects nine out of ten people with the disease and misses one. A high-sensitivity test is valuable when missing a disease would be serious, because a negative result then makes the disease unlikely.

sections.heading: Specificity
paragraphs: Specificity is the proportion of people without the disease whom the test correctly identifies as negative. A test with ninety percent specificity wrongly flags one in ten healthy people. A high-specificity test is useful to confirm a diagnosis, since a positive result is less likely to be a false alarm.

sections.heading: Why a positive result may be wrong
paragraphs: The chance that a positive result is correct depends on how common the disease is in the people tested. When a disease is rare, even a good test produces more false alarms than true cases. Imagine one thousand people, ten of whom have a disease. A test with ninety percent sensitivity and ninety percent specificity finds nine of the ten sick people, but also wrongly flags about ninety-nine of the nine hundred ninety healthy ones. Of about one hundred eight positives, only nine truly have the disease.

sections.heading: Consequences and questions
paragraphs: False positives cause anxiety and further tests, sometimes harmful ones. False negatives can delay treatment. Tests used for screening healthy people therefore need very high specificity, and a second, more specific test often follows a positive screening result.

Ask what the test is meant to show, how reliable it is for people like you, what a positive or negative result means for you and what happens next. Numbers out of one hundred are easier to understand than percentages.

sections.heading: Using this in everyday decisions
paragraphs: Knowing these terms helps when reading about new tests or screening programmes. A test advertised as ninety-nine percent accurate may still produce many false alarms when the condition is rare, so look for the numbers behind the claim.

examples.title: Making sense of a result
examples.text: Imagine your screening test is positive. You could ask what proportion of people with a positive result actually have the disease and what confirmatory test will follow.

examples.title: Comparing two tests
examples.text: Suppose you are offered two different tests. You might ask which is better at avoiding false alarms and which at avoiding missed cases, and why that matters for your situation.

questions: How accurate is this test, and what are its false-positive and false-negative rates?
What does a positive or negative result mean for me?
What would be the next step after an abnormal result?
